https://www.thetimes.com/article/nationa.title: National Portrait Gallery head says museums ‘can’t afford to be activists’
https://www.thetimes.com/article/nationa.subtitle: As the gallery unveils funding with links to big energy, its boss explains why
https://www.thetimes.com/article/nationa.text:
Museums cannot be activists, the director of the National Portrait Gallery has said, as he unveiled a replacement sponsor for BP: a legal firm with extensive links to big energy.
Nicholas Cullinan said that while the museum had “red lines” over who it would accept money from, the long-term dilution of government support had made it an “increasingly challenging” environment.
“I think you would be hard pressed to find any bank or law firm that didn’t have investments [in energy] so I think we just have to be careful because fundraising has always been about turning private wealth into public good and doing that while also acting in the public interest,” he told The Times.
“What you don’t want to do is start occupying that position of being an activist because it also puts off other people wanting to support museums.”
The gallery was one of the first to reject funding from members of the Sackler family, who made hundreds of millions of pounds from ownership of Purdue Pharma, which has been held responsible for fuelling the United States opioid crisis.
It began to distance itself from BP — which has sponsored its world- renowned portrait award for 30 years — in 2020, with the partnership coming to an end last year.
In the past five years BP, which has ploughed millions of pounds into Britain’s leading cultural institutions this century, has been dropped by almost every one, including the Royal Shakespeare Company and Tate.
Their decisions followed intense pressure from artists and activists claiming the company was fuelling the climate crisis and using cultural organisations to “greenwash” its reputation.
Today the gallery will unveil the international law firm Herbert Smith Freehills as the new headline sponsor for its internationally renowned painting competition, which has a £35,000 first prize.
However, the firm has extensive links with big energy and this year alone has advised two Chinese companies and an American one, all of which have substantial hydrocarbon interests.
Cullinan paid tribute to the company though and stressed the reliance of the state-funded museums which offer free entry — such as the gallery, the British Museum and Tate — on corporate donations. “It’s becoming increasingly challenging for museums to raise money especially in the UK. Each of us is only part-funded by government and the taxpayer. For us it is around 30 per cent. That is the direction of travel.
“It is a very fragile eco-system and you have to be very careful but you are always wanting to do what is, on balance, in the public good.”
Cullinan welcomed the return of the competition, now renamed the Herbert Smith Freehills Portrait Award, which will invite entries from artists aged 18 and over until January 16 next year.
The winner receives £35,000 — one of the largest prizes of any global arts competition — second place £12,000 and third place £10,000. There is also a £9,000 young artist prize for an entrant aged between 18 and 30. Because the gallery has been closed for an extensive redevelopment project since the beginning of the Covid-19 pandemic, artists are invited to submit work made since January 1, 2020.
The redevelopment, which was in part possible due to a large donation from the Blavatnik Foundation, set up by the Ukrainian-born billionaire Leonard Blavatnik, has been praised.
The response to the redevelopment, which included a substantial rehang, had been “phenomenal”, Cullinan said.
“In terms of visitor numbers we are on course for a record-breaking year,” he said, adding that visitor numbers were down across the board at other institutions. “The response from visitors has been overwhelmingly positive. We are very honest about Britain and its history; we don’t hide anything. But I think what comes across is a sense of hope and possibility.”
Other British museums to drop sponsorship deals include:
The V&A The Sackler name was removed from its galleries in London last year because of alleged links to the opioid addiction crisis in the US. The National Gallery, National Portrait Gallery and British Museum also dropped the name, as did the V&A in Dundee.
The National Galleries of Scotland severed its ties with BP in 2019, saying that it needed to “address the climate emergency”.
The Tate in London pleased campaigners when it was announced that BP was ending its sponsorship of the institution in 2017 after nearly three decades.
The National Gallery in London ended a 12-year corporate membership deal with Shell in 2018 and last had a sponsorship deal in 2015.
The Science Museum in London attracted criticism over a sponsorship deal with Shell for a 2021 exhibition exploring technologies to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and maintains relationships with other energy giants.
The Natural History Museum in London ended Shell’s sponsorship of its wildlife photography of the year award in 2008.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.title: Activists who disrupted race let off by judge who ‘understood why they did it’
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.subtitle: The climate protesters glued themselves to the track during a championship considered the pinnacle of cyclists’ careers
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.text:
Three climate change activists who disrupted an elite international cycling race by gluing themselves to the road have walked free from court after a sheriff said he understood why they had broken the law.
Sheriff Grant McCulloch merely admonished Catriona Roberts, 21, and Rebecca Kerr, 28 — both students — and Romane Moulin, 26, a renewable energy software developer, for forcing the UCI Cycling World Championships Men’s Elite Road Race, which was being televised worldwide, to pause for nearly an hour in August.
A fourth accused, Ben Taylor, 29, a carer, was fined £250 after the sheriff said that he was becoming “a professional protester”.
After a three-and-a-half hour trial, McCulloch ruled it was “obvious” that the actions of all four protesters, from the anti-oil group This is Rigged, amounted to a breach of the peace. He dismissed a submission from Taylor that his actions had been justified “like the suffragettes” by saying “the suffragettes were convicted”.
Falkirk sheriff court was told that the protesters, who had been spotted “dishevelled” and hiding in bushes beside the narrow road in the Carron Valley, Stirlingshire, before the UCI peloton was due to pass, took less than 30 seconds to set off pink powder cannons, pour glue on to their hands and stick themselves to the tarmac.
Taylor and Kerr sat back to back locked together by a cycling D-lock round their necks — the keys to which Taylor had thrown into the grass verge — and Moulin and Roberts locked themselves together with a large bike chain.
PC Gregor Malcolm, 53, a member of Police Scotland’s protester removal team, said: “The cyclists were incredibly upset. This was the peak of a lot of cyclists’ careers. It’s an individual event, which is unusual in cycling, so there was a lot of anger at being stopped. Many of these athletes train for years for a one-off race which can make or break their careers.”
Officers had to use a chemical de-bonder to release the group’s hands from the road, all of which took more than ten minutes.
The four accused said they were protesting about the involvement of petrochemical firms in the event and the granting of new licences for oil production in the North Sea, and denied a charge of breach of the peace.
McCulloch told Roberts, of Edinburgh; Taylor, of Kilbirnie in Ayrshire; and Moulin and Kerr, both of Glasgow: “Hundreds of cyclists had to grind to a halt on this narrow road because of the actions of four people. The potential for a serious disturbance is obvious ... I firmly accept that all four have firmly-held views and beliefs but protests must be proportionate and peaceful. This was the latter, but not the former.
“I clearly understand why the accused acted as they did. Indeed, many would think their actions to be applauded. Many would disagree and argue that such behaviour has no place in a democratic society. Miss Roberts, Miss Moulin and Miss Kerr — you are all admonished, as you are first offenders and I understand why you did what you did, although in my view it broke the law.” He fined Taylor, who has seven previous similar convictions in England, and told him: “You appear to be becoming a bit of an over-professional activist and protester.”
He earlier warned the demonstrators against “grandstanding”.
The race was won by the Dutch rider Mathieu van der Poel.
